Route 222 corridor, Latino businesses fuel regional, state economy
Legislative Latino Caucus co-hosts hearing at Latino Economic Summit
Rep. Johanny Cepeda-Freytiz
October 9, 2026 | 12:36 PM
READING, Oct. 9 –
Pennsylvania has the only growing economy in the Northeast, and Latino business owners and entrepreneurs are helping drive that economic engine. Rising costs that have hit residents particularly hard, including the rising cost for childcare and transportation, remain a challenge to continue growing the Pennsylvania’s workforce and economy.
“The Route 222 corridor has experienced a vast demographic transformation, and it has benefitted from this growth economically,” said state Rep. Johanny Cepeda-Freytiz, who represents portions of Berks County and serves as the Pennsylvania Legislative Latino Caucus chair. “Our young Latino population has faced challenges and obstacles, yet we have persevered to create better lives and stronger, safer neighborhoods.”
The Route 222 corridor links the cities and communities of Allentown, Bethlehem, Easton, Lancaster and Reading with the state’s youngest population. The hearing focused on the economy along the Route 222 corridor and was co-hosted by the Latino Caucus and the House Majority Policy Committee, with Latino Caucus chair Rep. Johanny Cepeda-Freytiz overseeing the hearing.
“What we heard today is Latinos have showed up and we will continue to show up for our community, creating jobs and helping drive economic growth in our region and across Pennsylvania,” said state Rep. Manny Guzman, who represents portions of Reading. “Unfortunately, we are going to be running into very lean years, because of the Big Beautiful Bill and the decision to slash the federal dollars that supported our communities.”
Small business owners asked the committee to create more opportunities for low-interest small business loans so new businesses don’t have to turn to using credit cards and their high-interest rates to create businesses and jobs.
“Latinos contribute more than we take and we improve the neighborhoods we call our home,” said state Rep. Danillo Burgos, who represents portions of Philadelphia. “We have generated job growth, paid taxes and made our neighborhoods better places to call home. The reality is we build, we invest and we create businesses that have helped revitalize Main streets and commercial spaces throughout Pennsylvania.”
The Route 222 corridor accounts for roughly 50% of Pennsylvania’s entire Latino population. Allentown Mayor Matt Tuerk noted the
Lehigh Valley’s economic growth
has the potential to advance across the Route 222 corridor.
The hearing took place during the
Route 222 Corridor Latino Economic Summit
in Reading.
“Latino entrepreneurs and family-owned Latino businesses are driving economic growth across the entire state,” said state Rep. Ryan Bizzarro, who represents portions of Erie County and serves as the House Majority Policy Committee chairman. “Greater access to capital for Latino entrepreneurs allows residents to keep their spending dollars in the local community – which only contributes to the growth of local jobs and wages.”
Friday
’s House Majority Policy hearing featured testimony from
Matt Tuerk
, the mayor for the city of Allentown;
Bryan Guzman
, the owner of
Innovation Cleaning
; and
Isamac Torres-Figueroa
, board president,
Berks County Latino Chamber of Commerce
.

Cepeda-Freytiz to host 2-day VSP Eyes of Hope Mobile Clinic event in Reading
Rep. Johanny Cepeda-Freytiz
October 2, 2026 | 2:25 PM
READING, Oct. 2 –
State Rep. Johanny Cepeda-Freytiz, D-Berks, along with VSP
®
Eyes of Hope, will host a two-day mobile vision clinic
from 9 a.m. – 5 p.m.
October 8 and 9
at
Centro Hispano Hispanic Center (25 N. 2nd St.)
to help Berks County children and adults receive free vision care and provide families with an opportunity to access state resources.
The event will feature a VSP
®
Eyes of Hope mobile vision clinic, which will provide free vision care for approximately 250 community members who do not have vision insurance and meet certain income guidelines.
“Access to vision care is crucial for everyone,” said Cepeda-Freytiz. “It’s especially important for young children to have access before they enter school. Glasses can help our children learn better and put them on the path to success in life, and a price tag should not keep them from achieving that success. This event will help ensure that children and their family members who otherwise may not be able to get glasses have what they need.”
Cepeda-Freytiz is the prime sponsor of
H.B. 1077
, legislation that would create a statewide commission to develop a plan that will ensure follow-up vision exams and glasses for all students in Pennsylvania. She also has introduced H.B. 1078, which would require comprehensive eye exams in school upon entry into a new school and at various grades that coincide with a child’s developmental stages.
Services for the mobile clinic are by appointment only. Eligible patients will have a family income up to 200% of the
federal poverty level guidelines
and be uninsured for vision care.
Registration can be completed
here
, or by calling Cepeda-Freytiz’s office at 484-577-2756.

House passes Alyssa’s Law to get panic alarms installed into schools
Legislation named in honor of student killed in Marjory Stoneman Douglas shooting
Rep. Johanny Cepeda-Freytiz
September 29, 2026 | 3:59 PM
HARRISBURG, Sept. 29 –
To ensure the safety of students and staff in schools across Pennsylvania, the state House has passed legislation introduced by state Rep. Johanny Cepeda-Freytiz, D-Berks, that would require schools to consider installing panic alarms to quickly respond to emergencies.
House Bill 634
would require schools to consider implementing a panic alarm system within their classrooms during annual safety and security reviews. These silent alarms would connect a specific classroom to law enforcement responders and signal a life-threatening emergency.
“Feeling safe in the classroom where they spend most of the year should be the bare minimum expectation that students, teachers and school staff have,” said Cepeda-Freytiz. “This legislation will take practical steps to ensure that in the case of a shooting or another emergency, law enforcement can act faster in these moments where every second used or wasted can mean the difference between life and death.”
The legislation, also known as Alyssa’s Law, has been backed by
Make Our Schools Safe
, which was founded by Lori and Ilan Alhadeff following the death of their 14-year-old daughter Alyssa in the 2018 Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School shooting.
“As Alyssa’s mother, I know firsthand that in an emergency, every second matters,” said
Lori Alhadeff
, co-founder and CEO of Make Our Schools Safe. “Alyssa’s Law is about giving teachers and school staff a direct, immediate way to call for help when lives are at risk. I am deeply grateful to Representative Johanny Cepeda-Freytiz for her leadership on H.B. 634 and for continuing to move this lifesaving legislation forward in Pennsylvania.
“No parent should ever have to experience the pain of losing a child in a place where they should be safe. By passing Alyssa’s Law, Pennsylvania has the opportunity to strengthen emergency response and help protect students and educators across the Commonwealth.”
“Being able to stand side-by-side with Lori and Ilan to advance this lifesaving legislation and having the opportunity to learn more about the incredible life that Alyssa lived has been deeply moving,” Cepeda-Freytiz said. “I am deeply grateful to the Alhadeffs for their work in Pennsylvania and across the nation to turn devastation and mourning into remembrance and action so that Alyssa is never forgotten and other families do not have to experience the same grief that they have.”
House Bill 634 will now advance to the state Senate for consideration. Pennsylvania is one of 14 states, in addition to the District of Columbia, with a version of Alyssa’s Law moving through the legislative process. If signed into law, Pennsylvania would join 13 other states, including Texas, Florida and New York, in putting a version of Alyssa’s Law on the books.

Salvation Army of Eastern PA awarded $250K to expand program aiding human trafficking victims
Rep. Johanny Cepeda-Freytiz
September 23, 2026 | 12:51 PM
HARRISBURG, Sept. 23 —
The Salvation Army of Eastern Pennsylvania has been awarded a state grant of $250,000 to expand an effective program that helps victims of human trafficking. The announcement was made today by state Reps. Jennifer O’Mara, D-Delaware, chair of the House Democratic Southeast Delegation; Johanny Cepeda-Freyitz, D-Berks, chair of the Pennsylvania Legislative Latino Caucus; and Manuel Guzman Jr., D-Berks.
The Salvation Army’s New Day to Stop Trafficking Program was established 15 years ago in Philadelphia and will be expanded across eastern Pennsylvania with the new grant.
The program provides critical services to victims of sex and labor trafficking, ensuring they have a safe and supportive environment as they transition toward a healthy future. Last year the program served more than 1,100 victims with trauma-informed case management, housing navigation and other essential support services.
“This program has a long track record of success,” O’Mara said. “Our delegation was fully supportive of this new funding, and we’re proud to see it come to fruition for communities across our region. The Salvation Army’s work is grounded in dignity, safety and the belief that every survivor deserves a chance to rebuild their lives on their own terms.”
“Our commonwealth has one of the highest numbers of human trafficking cases in the nation, and it takes place in every community, whether we can easily see it or not,” Cepeda-Freytiz said. “The work the Salvation Army has done in Philadelphia has been vital in supporting victims of this exploitation. I am glad to see this funding secured and look forward to seeing the New Day program expanded further into the state.”
“I’m pleased to see The Salvation Army’s New Day Program receive state funding to support its critical work combating human trafficking across Eastern Pennsylvania. I advocated for this funding because programs like New Day provide much-needed trauma-informed care, housing support and recovery services to survivors,” Guzman said. “This investment will help expand these resources and reach more communities. I thank The Salvation Army for its continued commitment to supporting survivors and strengthening our communities.”
The grant was awarded through a program at the state Department of Human Services.

Pennsylvania benefits from growing Latino population
Lawmakers listen as experts detail obstacles, challenges
Rep. Johanny Cepeda-Freytiz
September 22, 2026 | 12:43 PM
EASTON, Sept. 22
–
Pennsylvania’s growing Latino population is making important contributions to the commonwealth’s growing economy and workforce, while communities across the state continue working to address challenges facing Latino families and children.
The Pennsylvania Legislative Latino Caucus and House Majority Policy Committee today co-hosted a data-driven hearing on the state of the Latino community of Pennsylvania at the
Pennsylvania Latino Convention
in Easton.
“We are here to listen and learn what is working and what isn’t working, but more importantly, we are here to better understand what state lawmakers can do about it,” said Rep. Johanny Cepeda-Freytiz, who represents portions of Berks County and serves as the chairwoman of the Pennsylvania Legislative Latino Caucus. “The contributions of the Latino population to Pennsylvania are undeniable, but listening without action is just a conversation. We traveled here to learn more ideas and solutions, because our desire is to act.”
Experts detailed how Pennsylvania has welcomed Latinos into its workforce, a huge benefit in growing the state’s economy, but many times the children of Latino workers are struggling in the commonwealth’s education system.
“We heard it multiple times today: Pennsylvania has reaped incredible benefits from the Latino community, but we must do a better job serving our community and residents,” said Rep. Nikki Rivera, who represents portions of Lancaster County. “We are fighting for families like those we heard from today.”
Among the recommendations discussed during the hearing was the need to hire more bilingual teachers, bilingual teaching staff and bilingual school psychologists to better serve the state’s increasingly diverse schools.
“Pennsylvania’s Latino community is helping power our economy, strengthen our workforce and build stronger communities,” said Rep. Ryan Bizzarro, who serves as the House Majority Policy Committee chairman and represents portions of Erie County. “Our responsibility is to make sure every Latino family has a fair shot to succeed and the opportunity to thrive.”
Home ownership and income parity remain issues in the Latino community. Testifiers highlighted the growth of Pennsylvania’s youngest demographic, and its impressive number of entrepreneurs. However, the Latino population has the lowest median household income of any ethnic or racial group. Wages aren’t keeping pace with rising costs, squeezing workers and working families as communities are seeing an increase in food insecurity.
Consequently, the Latino population’s home ownership rate is below the state average, compounded by inequal access to credit for Latinos.
The event featured testimony from Chairman of the Pennsylvania Latino Convention
Norman Bristol Colon
(Lancaster); President of Pennsylvania Association of Hispanic School Administrators
Dr. Evelyn Nunez
; Chief of Personnel and External Relations, CHP Schools
Yemele Ayala
; Reading School Board member
Shaykayarira DelRio-
González
; Divisional Social Services Director, the Salvation Army
Heather LaRocca
; Executive Director of Hispanic Center Lehigh Valley
Raymond Santiago
; COO of APM Philadelphia
Manuel Delgado
; Legal Services Coordinator at
Casa San Jose
(Pittsburgh) Jorge Palmas; CEO
Capeles Agency
Angela Capeles
; and founder/president
La Promesa Foundation
Jesus Torres
.

.

Cepeda-Freytiz: ‘Over $1.4 million in new grants for our community’
Rep. Johanny Cepeda-Freytiz
September 15, 2026 | 10:50 AM
READING, Sept. 15 –
State Rep. Johanny Cepeda-Freytiz, D-Berks, has announced over $1.4 million in grant funding through the Local Share Account program that will benefit five projects in the 129th Legislative District.
“This funding will provide long-needed support for projects across our community, from helping our municipal governments and first responders to improving our greenways,” said Cepeda-Freytiz. “I look forward to seeing these projects come to fruition, and I will keep working to ensure that our community continues to get the state funding it deserves.”
The projects supported with this funding include:
$688,709
for the Schuylkill River Greenways Association to develop a trailhead at Buttonhead Road in Reading to connect with the River Trail.
$250,000
to Spring Township to add storage space in its Public Works building along Windmill Road.
$250,000
to renovate the Wyomissing Borough Fire Department Station, including the creation of individual sleeping quarters and bathrooms, exterior façade repairs and upgrades to plumbing, HVAC and electrical systems.
$160,000
to help construction in Sinking Spring through the purchase of a new wheel loader.
$104,328
for Opportunity House to replace the deteriorating roof of its main campus.
The
Local Share Account program
is funded through revenue generated by gaming and is administered by the Commonwealth Financing Authority to support projects that enhance economic development, public infrastructure and community vitality.

Rep. Johanny Cepeda-Freytiz
July 14, 2026
HARRISBURG, July 14 –
State Rep. Johanny Cepeda-Freytiz, chair of the PA Legislative Latino Caucus, celebrated the impact that the 2026-27 state budget will have on the district she represents in Berks County,
all without raising taxes
.
“We have achieved major wins that will help our neighbors here in Berks County and every community across Pennsylvania,” said Cepeda-Freytiz. “From education funding increases and requiring transparency around AI data centers to increasing affordable housing and putting money back in Pennsylvanians’ wallets, House Democrats delivered for all Pennsylvanians in this budget.”
This year’s budget will see $565 million
invested into schools across the state, with districts in Cepeda-Freytiz’s community seeing the following budget increases compared to last year:
Reading School District:
$28.5 million (9.7% increase)
Wilson School District:
$2.2 million (9.7% increase)
Wyomissing Area School District:
$171,000 (3.6% increase)
Other key highlights from the budget include:
Further investments in public education, school safety, special education, career training, higher education, career and technical education, STEM programs, and after school programs.
Putting $200 million back in the pockets of working Pennsylvanians through the Working Pennsylvanians Tax Credit.
Making sure everyone can afford to see a doctor when they get sick and improves care for our seniors.
Making our neighborhoods safer by giving law enforcement better tools to solve violent crimes and protect every Pennsylvanian.
Increasing affordable housing opportunities across the commonwealth.
Delivering a Cost-Of-Living-Adjustment and retirement security for teachers, police officers, firefighters, and other public servants who have not received one for 25 years.
Saving families money through tax relief and stronger consumer protections.
Modernizing government programs to better serve Pennsylvanians while improving transparency and accountability.
“The investments we made this year are historic for our state, but can go so much farther. As this legislative term moves forward, I will continue using my position, both as a legislator and as chair of the Legislative Latino Caucus, to push my colleagues in the Senate and across the aisle to act more for working Pennsylvanians and our state’s most vulnerable communities.”

Members of the legislative caucuses representing communities of color applaud Supreme Court decision in Trump v. Barbara
Calls for Continued Protection of Birthright Citizenship
Rep. Johanny Cepeda-Freytiz
June 30, 2026 | 11:27 AM
HARRISBURG, June 30 --
Today, the United States Supreme Court upheld the Constitution and reaffirmed the guarantee of birthright citizenship under the 14th Amendment—protecting thousands of Pennsylvania children born each year.
Every year, over 400,000 children are born to immigrant families in Pennsylvania. Today's decision reaffirms that children born in the U.S., who are raised here and pledge allegiance to our flag, are just as American as those born to citizens. This ruling ensures that these children, along with all children born on U.S. soil, will continue to be recognized as citizens with full rights and protections.
“This decision affirms what we have always known: that the Constitution does not discriminate,” said
Rep. Johanny Cepeda-Freytiz, chair of the Pennsylvania Legislative Latino Caucus
. “But while we celebrate today, we must remain vigilant. The rights of our communities should never be one court case away from being taken.”
“The fact that this administration saw fit to challenge a founding tenant of this nation, birthright citizenship, is an indictment of a racist, nationalist governing theology,” said
Rep. Napoleon Nelson, chair of the Pennsylvania Legislative Black Caucus
. “It is also a doomed governing theology that simply doesn’t understand that to be an American and to love this country does not rely on the country loving us back. America has never loved all of its citizens. Today’s SCOTUS ruling simply affirms the rights implied in our founding documents and inscribed into the Constitution in 1868.”
“Every American-born child deserves the legal rights, protections and liberties of citizenship. By recognizing this fact, we fulfill one of the most sacred promises of our country: that America can be a place of opportunity, freedom and a better life for generations,” said
Sen. Patty Kim, chair of the Pennsylvania Legislative Asian Pacific American Caucus
. “I am glad that the Supreme Court was on the right side of history today. However, as we breathe a collective sigh of relief, we must also remember that the rights of immigrants are still under attack every day. There is much more work to be done.”
“Birthright citizenship – recognizing that people born on U.S. soil are U.S. citizens – is a fundamental concept for American society and government. The United States was the first government to recognize that all people have inalienable rights at birth – and in doing so we rejected privileges based on aristocratic bloodlines. Birthright citizenship is the foundation of our democracy and our country’s place in the world. With it, we have become the greatest example of freedom and opportunity the world has ever seen,” said
Rep. Joseph Hohenstein, chair of the Welcoming PA Caucus.
“I am glad the Supreme Court reaffirmed this basic principle of our law and democratic form of government.”
This decision has immediate implications for classrooms across Pennsylvania. Thousands of students – especially in districts like Philadelphia, Reading, Allentown and Lancaster – will continue to have access to education, healthcare and economic opportunity without fear or uncertainty about their citizenship status.
But this moment demands action – not complacency.
The
legislative caucuses representing communities of color call on the:
U.S. House and Senate
to codify birthright citizenship into federal law and remove any ambiguity once and for all.

Measure creates pathway to help businesses get back on track with tax remittance obligations
Rep. Johanny Cepeda-Freytiz
June 8, 2026 | 4:33 PM
HARRISBURG, June 8 –
The Pennsylvania House today passed legislation introduced by state Rep. Johanny Cepeda-Freytiz, D-Berks, aimed at helping businesses with repeated sales tax filing issues become compliant and avoid falling deeper into tax delinquency.
The legislation,
H.B. 2300
, would require businesses that either have three non-consecutive non-filed returns or have a delinquent sales tax balance greater than $5,000 to use an authorized service provider to report and remit their sales tax.
“As a former small business owner myself, I know that balancing the books is vital for every business, regardless of how well a business owner can do that themselves,” said Cepeda-Freytiz. “This legislation will ensure 100% compliance with Pennsylvania’s sales tax collection and allow businesses to get back on track to continue serving our community.”
Prior to her election, Cepeda-Freytiz owned Mi Casa Su Casa Café, a breakfast and lunch café in downtown Reading.
The legislation would also require the Department of Revenue to cover the costs of this program for the taxpayer’s first year of enrollment.
House Bill 2300 passed the House with a vote of 153-48 and will now move to the state Senate for consideration.

Pennsylvania House passes bill to provide transparency in PUC records
Rep. Johanny Cepeda-Freytiz
June 3, 2026 | 3:05 PM
HARRISBURG, June 3 –
The Pennsylvania House has unanimously passed legislation that would provide greater transparency in the release of Public Utility Commission records in response to the 2023 West Reading R.M. Palmer chocolate factory explosion that killed seven people, announced state Rep. Johanny Cepeda-Freytiz, D-Berks.
After the explosion, the PUC, under
Act 156 of 2006
, was unable to give inspection reports with confidential security information to federal investigators who were seeking to find out the cause of the accident. The new proposal,
H.B. 306
, would authorize the PUC to share records containing such confidential information with federal agencies investigating safety issues.
“We should take every step to ensure that a tragedy like what occurred in my district in West Reading never happens again,” said Cepeda-Freytiz. “Statutory obstacles delayed the creation and release of the federal report into this tragedy, and we should not have to face any delays of this manner when we are working to solve a life-or-death issue.
“I am thankful to my House colleagues for taking action on this legislation, and several other natural gas safety bills I have introduced, so that families in my community are not just given words of support, but action so the loss of their loved ones are not in vain. I hope the Senate takes swift action to bring these bills to the governor’s desk.”
The legislation joins
three previously passed bills
introduced by Cepeda-Freytiz that would provide safeguards around natural gas, based on the causes of the R.M. Palmer explosion. These causes were outlined in a 2025
National Transportation Safety Board report
, two years after the incident.
House Bill 306, as well as Cepeda-Freytiz’s other three bills, await consideration in the state Senate.

Bill to ensure student access to eyeglasses passed by State House
Rep. Johanny Cepeda-Freytiz
May 4, 2026 | 3:41 PM
HARRISBURG, May 4 –
The Pennsylvania House has passed legislation that would establish a Commission on Children’s Vision to ensure that all students have access to eyeglasses, according to the bill’s prime sponsor, state Rep. Johanny Cepeda-Freytiz, D-Berks.
House Bill 1077
would establish a commission within the Department of Health, made up of the secretaries of Education and Health, along with several healthcare and community representatives, to create a statewide plan to ensure that all students who need follow-up vision examinations have glasses and ensure this comes at little to no cost for the student or their family.
“Vision problems can have lifelong impacts, especially on our students,” said Cepeda-Freytiz, who wears glasses herself. “Unaddressed vision problems can cause headaches and a lack of focus in class and can even impact grades. Many students are misidentified as having behavioral issues or are placed on IEPs when all they need are eyeglasses.
“The benefits of glasses in the classroom translate to success outside of the classroom. We are working to ensure that our students have access to the resources they need to see a successful future.”
The legislation is similar to the Children’s Vision Strike Force launched in Ohio in 2024, which brings together health and education professionals to ensure that students have access to eyeglasses.
The bill passed the House, 150-51, and now moves to the state Senate for consideration. The commission’s first meeting would be held within 30 days of the legislation being enacted.

Legislation to expand event permits statewide introduced in PA House
Would let all Pennsylvania municipalities expand alcohol sales during World Cup and national anniversary celebrations
Rep. Johanny Cepeda-Freytiz
April 29, 2026 | 9:31 AM
HARRISBURG, April 29 –
As Pennsylvania prepares for a busy tourism season, including major celebrations of America’s 250th anniversary, recognition of the anniversary of the Battle of Gettysburg, and hosting several World Cup games, state Rep. Johanny Cepeda-Freytiz, D-Berks, has introduced legislation that would allow all municipalities across Pennsylvania to expand their event permits during this period.
The bill,
H.B. 2471
, would replicate on a statewide level similar bipartisan legislation,
Act 8 of 2026
, which allows bars in Philadelphia to continue serving alcohol until 4 a.m. from June 11 to July 20, 2026. Act 8 was signed into law by Gov. Josh Shapiro two weeks after being introduced.
“Between the World Cup and America 250 celebrations, southeastern Pennsylvania alone is expected to generate $2 billion to $3 billion,” said Cepeda-Freytiz, “However, tourism will not just be contained in Philadelphia – tourists will be visiting World Cup Fan Zones in Reading, Scranton and Pittsburgh, while also visiting landmarks such as Valley Forge and Gettysburg.
“If we are providing one municipality with the tools to expand its local economy, I believe every municipality should be able to prime their local events and businesses accordingly. We are set for a tourism season that will welcome hundreds of thousands of visitors, so we should act to provide the greatest experience that every part of Pennsylvania can offer.”
The permits would allow businesses in good standing to pay a $500 application fee to stay open and continue serving alcohol until 4 a.m. as opposed to the current limit of 2 a.m. to accommodate soccer games held in different time zones.
This legislation, similar to the already-passed law for Philadelphia, would only apply during the one-month period including the World Cup. House Bill 2471 has not yet been assigned to a committee for consideration.

Cepeda-Freytiz, Burgos introduce legislation to mark Colombian Independence Day
Rep. Johanny Cepeda-Freytiz
April 20, 2026 | 3:28 PM
HARRISBURG, April 20 –
To commemorate when patriot leaders set into motion events that led to independence in Colombia 216 years ago, state Reps. Johanny Cepeda-Freytiz, D-Berks, and Danilo Burgos, D-Phila., have introduced legislation that would recognize Colombian Independence Day in Pennsylvania.
The legislation,
H.R. 487
, would recognize July 20, 2026, as Colombian Independence Day. On July 20, 1810, the struggle for Colombian independence began in Santafé de Bogotá, shaping Latin American and world history.
“The road to Colombia’s independence began as a movement for local self-government and continued to grow over the next decade,” said Cepeda-Freytiz, who chairs the Pennsylvania Legislative Latino Caucus. “This ultimately led to the formation of the Republic of Gran Colombia, which supported the independence of many other Latin American nations.
“This resolution will honor that momentous legacy, the longstanding ties between our Commonwealth and Colombia, and the contributions Colombians have made to enrich Pennsylvania’s economy, civic life, and culture.”
“Pennsylvania holds a unique place in the story of Colombian independence, acting as an early hub where revolutionary ideas were shared and strengthened,” said Burgos. “Recognizing Colombian Independence Day is not only a tribute to the courage and determination of those who fought for freedom, but also a celebration of the deep historical ties we share.”
Pennsylvania and Colombia share a connected history of independence, with Philadelphia serving as a hub for the Colombian independence movement. Its ports, printers, merchants, and political circles helped circulate the ideas that inspired Colombian revolutionaries.

Legislation to recognize Venezuelan Independence Day introduced in state House
Rep. Johanny Cepeda-Freytiz
April 20, 2026 | 3:23 PM
HARRISBURG, April 20 –
To mark the nation’s 215th anniversary, state Reps. Johanny Cepeda-Freytiz, D-Berks, and Danilo Burgos, D-Phila., have introduced legislation that would recognize Venezuelan Independence Day in Pennsylvania.
The legislation,
H.R. 486
, would recognize July 5, 2026, as Venezuelan Independence Day. Venezuela became the first nation in the Americas to declare independence from Spain on July 5, 1811, which led to a wave of independence movements across Latin America.
“Venezuela’s long-fought war for independence marked extraordinary courage and sacrifice that reshaped world history,” said Cepeda-Freytiz, who chairs the Pennsylvania Legislative Latino Caucus. “Venezuelan independence led other Latin American nations to seek independence, and the Venezuelan community in both their nation and Pennsylvania continues to shape the future.
“I am honored to lead this effort to commemorate this historic day and uplift the contributions Venezuelans have made to our Commonwealth.”
"Recognizing Venezuelan Independence Day here in Pennsylvania is a powerful way to honor the resilience, courage, and spirit of the Venezuelan people,” said Burgos. “Their fight for freedom not only shaped a nation, but inspired movements across the continent. I’m proud to recognize and celebrate the vibrant Venezuelan community right here in Pennsylvania, whose cultural and economic contributions continue to strengthen our Commonwealth.”
Pennsylvania and Venezuela share a connected history of independence, with many revolutionary ideas that inspired Venezuela’s independence movement coming out of Philadelphia.
This history is reflected today with Venezuelan revolutionary Francisco de Miranda, an acquaintance of George Washington, having a statue outside the Franklin Institute in Philadelphia. The statue was gifted to the city by the government of Venezuela in 1977.
The Legislative Latino Caucus plans to recognize
Venezuelan Independence Day with a celebration on June 17 in the state Capitol
. More details about this event will be available at a later date.

PA House passes third natural gas safety bill after R.M. Palmer factory tragedy
Comes in response to factory explosion in Cepeda-Freytiz’s district
Rep. Johanny Cepeda-Freytiz
April 15, 2026 | 3:32 PM
HARRISBURG, April 15 –
The Pennsylvania House today passed a bill introduced by state Rep. Johanny Cepeda-Freytiz, D-Berks, that would address safety concerns in workplaces that use natural gas, in response to the R.M. Palmer factory tragedy that occurred in West Reading in March 2023.
The legislation,
H.B. 1522
, would require the installation of natural gas alarms in businesses, residences and other buildings that use natural gas.
This measure follows
findings
that a natural gas leak was a root cause of the explosion at the West Reading chocolate factory—an explosion that claimed seven lives and injured 10 others in Cepeda-Freytiz’s legislative district.
“Three years after this tragedy, and one year after the investigation concluded, we have now passed the final bill addressing its cause,” Cepeda-Freytiz said. “There is an empty space in our community left by the seven lives we lost that day. Their families deserve action—action that ensures no other community has to endure the same heartbreak. I will continue to push for these bills as they move through the Senate.”
House Bill 1522 is the third and final piece of a legislative package introduced by Cepeda-Freytiz in response to the causes of the West Reading tragedy.
The other two bills are
H.B. 1525
, which would require the owners and operators of pipelines transporting steam in public rights-of-way to register the lines with the Pennsylvania One Call System, and
H.B. 1526
, which would require the Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission to work with natural gas pipeline operators to develop guidance and management programs to address potential threats to degrading plastic pipelines.
All three bills passed the House with bipartisan support and have been sent to the state Senate for consideration. House Bills 1525 and 1526 are awaiting consideration by the Senate Consumer Protection & Professional Licensure Committee, while H.B. 1522 has not yet been assigned to a committee.

Legislative Latino Caucus welcomes Tiburcio as newest member
Rep. Johanny Cepeda-Freytiz
March 23, 2026 | 4:31 PM
HARRISBURG, March 23 –
The Pennsylvania Legislative Latino Caucus, chaired by state Rep. Johanny Cepeda-Freytiz, today issued the following statement welcoming state Rep. Ana Tiburcio, D-Lehigh, as the newest member of the caucus:
“It is an honor to welcome Representative Tiburcio to the House and the Legislative Latino Caucus to serve as a powerful voice for Lehigh County,” said Cepeda-Freytiz, D-Berks. “She brings a wealth of personal and professional experience to Harrisburg, and she will greatly improve the impact of our collective advocacy to fight for the Latino community and all Pennsylvanians.”
Tiburcio was sworn in today after being elected in February to fill the seat vacated by Josh Siegel following his election as Lehigh County Executive. She will serve until the current term ends in December 2026.
Tiburcio’s swearing-in brings the number of House members of Latino descent up to eight, with Tiburcio being the only one currently from the Lehigh Valley region. She is also the fourth Dominican American elected to the House, after state Reps. Danilo Burgos, Manuel Guzman, and Cepeda-Freytiz.
Prior to her election, Tiburcio was the owner of A&M Tax & Services, a former school board director of the Allentown School District, and served as a program coordinator for the Fine Feather Foundation, a nonprofit empowering youth through creativity, education, and mentorship. She is also involved with Allentown Works, the Allentown city beautification project Love Your Block, and Allentown Blueprint Communities.
The 22nd Legislative District is nearly 61% Hispanic, the second-highest percentage of any House district in Pennsylvania.
